memory_update.text: PANW should be treated as the primary public-market consolidator candidate for the node after the February 11, 2026 CyberArk acquisition added identity, privileged access, machine identity, and agentic identity exposure to its network/cloud/security-operations platform.
CRWD maps to endpoint-led security telemetry that expands into cloud, identity, asset visibility, managed detection/response, and next-generation SIEM.
ZS maps to zero-trust/SASE/SSE demand for distributed users, devices, workloads, and applications; it should be evaluated against PANW, Cloudflare, Netskope/private, and hyperscaler-native offerings.

OKTA remains a direct identity-security candidate, especially for workforce/customer identity and emerging AI-agent identity, but competitive validation versus Microsoft Entra and PANW/CyberArk is required.

FROG is a less obvious but high-relevance software-supply-chain candidate because artifact repositories, binary governance, SBOM generation/consumption, and dependency controls may become compliance evidence layers.

Important near-miss candidates not included due to the five-name limit: Microsoft for Entra/Defender/GitHub/Azure security, Cloudflare for Zero Trust and application/API security, Fortinet for network/SASE/security fabric, GitLab for DevSecOps and secure software development, Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7 for vulnerability exposure management, SentinelOne for endpoint/XDR, Rubrik for cyber resilience, Check Point for platform security, and Dynatrace/Datadog/Splunk/Cisco for security observability/SIEM adjacencies.
FROG and GTLB are the cleanest public-market mappings for software-supply-chain assurance and secure-by-design implementation because they sit inside the software build/release lifecycle.

PANW and CRWD represent platform-consolidation candidates rather than pure supply-chain-assurance vendors; include them when the funnel is testing whether security spend consolidates around broad control planes.
TENB is a second-order regulated-input/data-provider candidate: exposure and vulnerability intelligence can feed compliance, SBOM consumption, and remediation-evidence workflows.

OKTA is highly relevant to identity and AI-agent governance but was not included in the five-candidate list due to the candidate cap; revisit if the next pass focuses specifically on identity, non-human identities, and AI-agent access governance.

Private or acquired chokepoint vendors such as Snyk, Wiz/Google, Venafi/CyberArk/PANW, GitHub/Microsoft, HashiCorp/IBM, Sonatype, Black Duck, Chainguard, and Anchore may be important ecosystem references even when they are not standalone US-listed equities.

PANW should remain in the node universe as the platform-consolidation and AI/machine-identity leader after the February 11, 2026 CyberArk close; map it to identity, cloud security, SASE, SOC automation, CNAPP, and AI security rather than only firewall exposure.
FROG is a high-specificity software-supply-chain candidate: artifact registry, package governance, SBOM/provenance/security scanning, and potential AI model/MCP artifact governance.
GTLB is a DevSecOps/software-factory candidate where AI coding, secure-by-design, compliance evidence, and software-supply-chain controls converge inside the SDLC workflow.

The node should be split in later layers into at least six subnodes: identity/machine identity, SASE/Zero Trust/API edge, CNAPP/cloud workload security, DevSecOps/AppSec, artifact/SBOM/SCA/provenance, and exposure/vulnerability management.
Need next-pass checks on CRWD, ZS, OKTA, DDOG, QLYS, RBRK, IBM/HashiCorp, MSFT/GitHub, ORCL, and federal/defense cyber integrators; omitted here due to five-candidate cap.
